title: Why Airplane Windows Are Round (It Cost 56 Lives)

shots.vo: January, nineteen fifty-four. Thirty-five people are flying over the Mediterranean, in the most advanced airliner on Earth. They have no idea they have seconds to live.
shots.prompt: wide shot, a 1950s silver four-engine jet airliner breaking apart in mid-air high above a calm blue Mediterranean sea, debris and smoke trails, distant view, clear daylight

shots.vo: Three months later, another one falls. Fifty-six people dead. No storm. No bomb. No explanation.
shots.prompt: interior, empty 1950s airliner passenger cabin, rows of vintage seats, sunlight beams through square windows, dust in the air, no people

shots.vo: The killer was never hidden. In fact, you have probably touched it.
shots.prompt: over-the-shoulder view from a modern airplane seat, oval cabin window with rounded corners, airplane wing outside above white clouds

shots.vo: It is right next to your seat, every time you fly. Do you know what it is?
shots.prompt: close-up, a single oval airplane window with rounded corners inside a dark cabin, one beam of light shining through

shots.vo: Your window. Look at its shape. Why is it never square? Not on one passenger jet, anywhere in the world.
shots.prompt: interior, a row of oval windows along the wall of a modern airliner cabin, soft warm reading lights, empty seats

shots.vo: Most people think it is about style. It is not. That gentle curve exists because people died.
shots.prompt: back view silhouette of a traveler with headphones looking out of an oval airplane window at clouds, face not visible

shots.vo: To find out who, and why, we have to go back to a plane that was supposed to change everything.
shots.prompt: 1950s silver jet airliner parked on an empty airfield at dawn, four engines inside the wings, long row of large square windows on the fuselage, low angle

shots.vo: May, nineteen fifty-two. The de Havilland Comet carries its first paying passengers. The first jet airliner in history. The whole world is watching.
shots.prompt: 1950s silver jet airliner taking off from a runway, crowd of people in 1950s coats watching behind a wire fence, morning

shots.vo: It flies almost twice as high as the propeller planes of its day. Above the storms. Above the turbulence. Above everything.
But up there, the air is too thin to breathe. So the cabin is pumped full of air, until the whole fuselage swells like a balloon. Every single flight. Remember that.
And along its sides? Big, beautiful, almost square windows. Passengers love them. Nobody sees the danger.
shots.prompt: interior, 1950s jet airliner cabin, large almost square windows, passengers in 1950s suits and hats seated, soft focus faces, warm light

shots.vo: The tenth of January, nineteen fifty-four. B. O. A. C. Flight seven eight one takes off from Rome, bound for London.
shots.prompt: 1950s silver jet airliner climbing over the Italian coast in morning light, the city of Rome far below, aerial view

shots.vo: Minutes later, near the island of Elba, it simply comes apart in the sky. All thirty-five people on board are killed.
shots.prompt: aerial view of the island of Elba in a calm turquoise sea, a thin trail of smoke in an empty sky above it, somber

shots.vo: Fishermen look up, and see pieces of the plane falling into the sea.
shots.prompt: 1950s Italian wooden fishing boats on a calm sea, fishermen standing in the boats looking up at the sky, seen from behind

shots.vo: Investigators guess. A fire? An engine? They make a few changes, and the Comets are flying again. A decision that would kill twenty-one more people.
shots.prompt: 1950s aircraft engineers in overalls inspecting an open jet engine bay inside a hangar, work lamps, toolboxes

shots.vo: The eighth of April. Barely two weeks after the jets returned. South African Airways Flight two oh one leaves Rome for Cairo.
shots.prompt: 1950s silver jet airliner climbing into an orange evening sky over the coast of southern Italy, side view

shots.vo: Near Naples, it vanishes from the sky. Twenty-one more lives. Gone.
shots.prompt: the Bay of Naples at dusk, Mount Vesuvius on the horizon, an empty darkening sky, still water, haunting mood

shots.vo: Two identical planes. Two perfect days. The same airport. The same terrifying ending. So what is ripping them apart?
The Comet is grounded. And Britain launches one of the biggest crash investigations the world has ever seen.
shots.prompt: high angle, 1950s investigation hall, long tables covered with twisted aluminium wreckage, investigators in suits and white lab coats

shots.vo: The Royal Navy drags the seabed off Elba, pulling up the broken jet, piece by piece.
shots.prompt: 1950s Royal Navy salvage ship at sea, a crane lifting a twisted piece of metal fuselage out of the water, grey sky

shots.vo: At Farnborough, they rebuild it like a giant puzzle. But the one piece that could explain everything is still at the bottom of the sea.
shots.prompt: inside a huge hangar, reassembled wreckage of a silver airliner fuselage on a wooden frame, missing pieces, engineers with clipboards

shots.vo: So the investigators try something insane. Something nobody has ever done.
shots.prompt: inside a hangar, a complete silver 1950s airliner fuselage being lowered by cranes into a giant rectangular water tank

shots.vo: They put an entire airliner into a giant tank of water. And they fly it. Over and over. Without it ever leaving the ground.
shots.prompt: a 1950s airliner fuselage submerged in a massive water tank, pipes and pumps around it, engineers watching from a walkway

shots.vo: Water is pumped in to stretch the cabin, exactly like a flight at cruising height. Then released. Then again. Every cycle, one flight.
Day and night, the tank keeps flying. And then, after about three thousand flights' worth of cycles, the fuselage rips open.
shots.prompt: underwater inside a giant test tank, a long jagged split tearing open the riveted aluminium skin of an airliner fuselage, bubbles escaping, dramatic light

shots.vo: Look where the crack begins. Not in the middle of the metal. At a corner. The sharp corner of a square opening.
shots.prompt: extreme close-up of a flat riveted aluminium panel with one square window cut-out, a single thin dark crack running diagonally away from its sharp top corner, rows of rivets, studio light
shots.negative: airplane, aircraft, jet, wing, fuselage, holes, rust, organic, leaf, mud, skin

shots.vo: Why a corner? When the cabin swells, the metal around every opening is pulled tight. Around a smooth curve, that force flows evenly.
But a sharp corner traps it. All that force piles into one tiny point, pulling far harder than anywhere else on the plane.
Every flight stretches that point a little more. Not enough to break. Just enough to weaken it. Again. And again.
Engineers call it metal fatigue. A crack too small to see, growing silently, flight after flight. Until one day, the metal gives up.
shots.prompt: macro close-up of a smooth polished aluminium sheet with neat rows of rivets, a hairline fatigue crack spreading from one rivet hole across the metal, cold metallic light
shots.negative: airplane, aircraft, jet, wing, fuselage, holes, rust, organic, leaf, mud, skin

shots.vo: And at cruising height, a pressurised cabin does not leak. It bursts outward, in a fraction of a second.
Then a missing piece of the Elba jet is pulled from the sea. A section of the roof. The break had started at the corner of a small square opening. The tank was right.
shots.prompt: a piece of salvaged silver aircraft roof panel on a wooden workbench, a small square hole cut in the metal with one corner torn open, rivet rows, a desk lamp, investigators' tools
shots.negative: holes, rust, organic, leather, cloth, green

shots.vo: The verdict changed aviation forever. When the Comet finally flew again, years later, its windows were oval.
shots.prompt: 1950s-style silver jet airliner with oval windows flying above sunlit clouds, hopeful bright mood, side view

shots.vo: Today every airliner on Earth has rounded windows, so the force flows around them, instead of piling up in one deadly point.
Right now, thousands of planes above you are swelling and shrinking with every flight. And they hold.
shots.prompt: modern passenger jet at an airport gate at night, cabin lights glowing through its row of oval windows, wet tarmac reflections

shots.vo: Because of a lesson learned in nineteen fifty-four.
shots.prompt: inside a modern airplane, close-up of the rounded corner of a cabin window frame, the engine and wing visible outside, soft light

shots.vo: So next time you rest your head against that little oval window, ask yourself: who paid for its shape? Fifty-six people did.
shots.prompt: a child's small hand touching an oval airplane window, sunset clouds outside, warm amber light

shots.vo: And that is the hidden why.
